      • 16. Orbits, stabilizers, and Burnside’s lemma

      16. Orbits, stabilizers, and Burnside’s lemma#

      A necklace is made by placing beads at equally spaced positions around a circle. Two arrangements of colored beads give the same necklace if one can be rotated into the other. This note counts necklaces, and more generally colorings up to the symmetries in a group, using the groups of Lecture Note 14 and the cosets of Lecture Note 15. We start with a problem small enough to solve by listing.

      Problem 1 (Necklaces with four beads)#

      How many different necklaces can be made from beads, each black or white, if two necklaces are the same when one can be rotated into the other?

      We number the bead positions counterclockwise, like the corners of the square, and record an arrangement as the string of colors in positions . There are strings. The rotations of the square form the group , and rotating an arrangement moves each bead to a new position, which for the identity is the same position. Figure 1 sorts the strings into classes of strings that can be rotated into one another. There are classes, so there are necklaces.

      A tempting shortcut is to divide: there are strings and rotations, so perhaps there are necklaces. This uses the division rule from Unit I, which requires every necklace to be represented by the same number of strings. Here the classes have , , or strings: BWBW looks the same after a half turn, so only strings represent its necklace, and BBBB is represented by only . The division undercounts because symmetric necklaces have fewer representatives. This note explains how the class sizes are determined and how to count classes without listing them.

      After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

      • Describe how a group acts on a set of colorings, and compute the result of moving a coloring by a group element.

      • Compute orbits and stabilizers, and use the orbit–stabilizer theorem to find orbit sizes.

      • State and prove Burnside’s lemma by counting pairs in two ways.

      • Count the colorings fixed by a permutation using its number of cycles.

      • Count necklaces and bracelets with beads and colors.

      16.1 Groups acting on sets#

      16.1.1 Actions#

      In Problem 1, each symmetry of the square moves each string of colors to another string. This is a second way in which the same group rearranges a set: the group permutes the positions, and it also permutes the colorings. The following definition covers both.

      16.2 Orbits#

      In Figure 1, each column collects the colorings that can be reached from one of them by rotations. In the language of actions, such a column is an orbit.

      Definition 8 (Orbit)#

      Let act on . The orbit of is the set of all elements to which can be moved:

      The columns of Figure 1 are the orbits of the colorings under . A necklace is such an orbit (the general definition follows below), so counting necklaces means counting orbits. For this count to make sense, each coloring must lie in exactly one orbit.

      Proposition 9 (Orbits do not overlap)#

      Every lies in its own orbit . If two orbits have an element in common, then they are equal.

      Proof#

      Since , we have .

      Suppose , so for some . Moving both sides by gives . Then for every , So . Exchanging the roles of and gives the reverse inclusion.

      So the different orbits split into disjoint blocks. Two colorings in the same orbit are called equivalent under .

      Definition 10 (Necklaces and bracelets)#

      Place positions counterclockwise around a circle, at the corners of a regular -gon. A necklace with beads and colors is an orbit of the colorings of the positions under the rotation group . A bracelet is an orbit under the dihedral group .

      A bracelet can be turned over as well as rotated, so two colorings that are mirror images of each other give the same bracelet but may give different necklaces.

      16.4 Burnside’s lemma#

      We want the number of orbits, and the orbits may have different sizes. The orbit–stabilizer theorem gives each orbit’s size in terms of stabilizers, and we use it to count orbits by counting pairs in two ways.

      Theorem 16 (Burnside’s lemma)#

      Let a finite group act on a finite set . The number of orbits is

      The sum is over the elements of the group, not over the elements of . In words: the number of orbits is the average, over all , of the number of elements of that leaves unchanged.

      Step 4: Conclusion.

      Comparing Steps 1 and 3, . Dividing by gives the formula.

      In Step 3, a large orbit contains many elements, each with a small stabilizer, and a small orbit contains few elements, each with a large stabilizer. In both cases the orbit contributes exactly pairs to , which is why unequal orbit sizes do not spoil the count.

      16.5 Fixed colorings and cycles#

      With Theorem 19, Burnside’s lemma needs only the number of cycles of each group element.

      16.7 Counting bracelets#

      A bracelet is an orbit under , which contains the rotations and the reflections described in Lecture Note 14. The rotations contribute the same terms as for necklaces. Each reflection has cycles of length and only, and the number of its fixed points was found there:

      • if is odd, each reflection has fixed point and cycles of length , so cycles in all;

      • if is even, half of the reflections have fixed points and cycles of length , so cycles in all, and the other half have cycles of length and no fixed points.
